newsitem.title: USA: Western U.S. utility mergers, alliances expected.
newsitem.headline: Western U.S. utility mergers, alliances expected.

text.p: The accelerating pace of electricity deregulation in western U.S. states is expected to spur more mergers and alliances between utilities and other power industry participants.

Industry experts say plans by California to begin opening the state's huge electricity market to outside suppliers no later than January 1998 have enhanced the appeal of western utilities as partners for other energy companies.
They cited the planned acquisition by Enron Corp. of Portland General Corp. as a pattern likely to be repeated, with PacifiCorp and Washington Water Power Co. viewed as especially eligible.

"A lot of big marketers are looking at northwestern utilities," said one Washington state utility source. "They have a vast amount of cheap generation and access to BPA (Bonneville Power Administration) transmission."
In addition, regulatory and financial concerns were expected to limit the appeal of some other electric utilities as merger candidates.

"PG&E (Pacific Gas and Electric Co. and Edison (Edison International's Southern California Edison Co. still have nuclear assets hanging over their heads," noted a California-based utility executive."They would bring a lot of baggage along with them."
Nuclear power, once deemed a cheap source of electricity, has become a high-cost albatross for U.S. utilities that have invested in the environmentally-plagued power source.
Despite its huge size and potential regulatory issues raised by its leverage over transmission, PacifiCorp, based in Portland, Ore., was at the top of many lists as ripe for further expansion.

"We are very growth oriented," said PacifiCorp spokesman Dave Kvamme, noting that the company's 1989 merger with Utah Power and Light was the first electric utility merger of any significance in the industry for 30 years.
"Our reasons for merging then were the very same reasons people are looking to merge right now--lower costs and better service for customers."

PacifiCorp has moved aggressively to establish a national presence with actions such as an agreement to sell power produced by Kentucky's Big Rivers Electric Corp., a type of partnership which it views as a good model for the future, said Kvamme.
But PacifiCorp "is still lacking on the gas side," said the California utility source. "If I had to bet, PacifiCorp would be next."

A merger or alliance involving PacifiCorp is "very possible," said Lesa Sroufe, research analyst at Ragen MacKenzie. "They have been more active in acquiring assets than most utilities over the last decade and will likely continue."
Washington Water Power Co., which saw a long-awaited merger with Sierra Pacific succomb to regulatory concerns earlier this year, was also touted as a likely merger candidate.
"Washington Water Power is a prime target now that its merger with Sierra Pacific has gone by the wayside," said another industry source.
A spokeswoman at WWP said the utility is working to establish a national presence on its own, but may consider other merger partners or strategic partnerships.
"We are looking at expanding regionally and nationally," said spokeswoman Susan Nielsen. "We want to grow our customer base in a variety of different ways."

The Spokane, Wash.-based utility already has a national retail unit, is moving aggressively to expand wholesale sales, and this week received Federal Energy Regulatory Commission approval for a wholesale power marketing subsidiary.
"WWP is a low-cost electric power supplier with sizable gas business. It is attractive both as a stand-alone entity and as a merger partner," said Ragen MacKenzie's Sroufe.

Also in the Northwest, shareholders of Seattle-based Puget Sound Power and Light and Washington Energy approved merging to form a combined gas/electric utility, but state regulators have yet to approve the deal.
